entries.meaning: The vessel preposition. It began as sailors' vocabulary and spread to trains, buses, planes, and spacecraft, keeping its slightly formal flavor the whole way. Its figurative use — joining a crew, and so joining a company or a project — is now common in business English, but almost always as the adverb (welcome aboard) rather than with an object.
examples: We climbed aboard the trawler before sunrise. (1)
They loaded the horses aboard the transport one at a time. (1)
Everyone aboard the train felt the jolt. (2)
The instruments aboard the probe are still returning data. (2)
Two of the three crew members aboard the vessel were rescued. (2)
He came aboard the firm as a junior partner. (3)
She brought two of her old analysts aboard the project with her. (3)
Compare the two-word idiom: we need the union on board before we announce anything. (agreement — not this preposition)

body: The passengers filed aboard the ferry.

senses.head: Position on a vessel or vehicle
body: There were nineteen people aboard the flight.

entries.русский: на борт, на борту — только о судне, самолёте, поезде; и движение, и положение сразу
entries.register: neutral, but tied to transport; formal or ceremonial outside it
entries.type: compound (a- "on" + board, fused — the board is a ship's side)
entries.complement: noun phrase only — a vehicle or vessel. No gerunds, no clauses, no ordinary places: aboard the terminal is wrong. It is also a bare adverb with no object at all (All aboard!, Welcome aboard), which is the usual test for telling the two uses apart.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] aboard [vessel / vehicle] · [verb] [object] aboard [vessel / vehicle] · aboard [vessel / vehicle], [main clause]
entries.contrast: Aboard covers both the motion and the resulting position, so it does the work of onto and on at once — but only for craft. Everyday American English says get on the plane; climb aboard the plane is the heightened or official register (announcements, journalism, nautical writing). The spelling trap: the figurative "in agreement" sense is two words — get everyone on board with the plan, never onboard or aboard — while onboard as one word is an adjective for equipment (onboard navigation).
entries.see also: onto, on, into, off, upon

entries.meaning: Motion that terminates in forcible contact, or motion that pushes back on an opposing force. The static "leaning" sense is really the resting state left behind by that motion, which is why the same word covers both. From there the meaning generalizes to opposition of every kind — political, legal, and physical — and finally to a backdrop, where one thing is seen pressed up against another.
examples: The rain beat against the windshield the whole way home. (1)
He kicked the ball against the garage door until his mother made him stop. (1)
She leaned her shoulder against the doorframe and waited. (2)
Two rakes stood against the shed. (2)
Walking against that wind was like walking uphill. (3)
The salmon fight their way against the current for miles. (3)
Every senator from the state voted against the bill. (4)
Her lawyer advised against saying anything publicly. (4)
The lighthouse showed white against the storm clouds. (5)
His accent stood out against everyone else's. (5)
The clinic vaccinates against four strains. (6)
We're insured against flood but not against fire. (6)

body: The hail rattled against the skylight.

senses.head: Resting contact under pressure

senses.head: Seen with something behind it

entries.pronunciation note: uh-GENST; also /əˈɡeɪnst/ uh-GAYNST (minority American, standard British); casual /əˈɡɛns/ — uh-GENS, with the final t dropped before a consonant (against the wall)
entries.русский: об, о (с силой) — соприкосновение с нажимом; против (противодействие); на фоне чего-то
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (advised against going) — never a finite clause. Write against the idea that he was lying, not against he was lying.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] against [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] against [noun phrase] · against [verb-ing] · stranded: the wall he threw it against
entries.contrast: Against is the contact-with-force preposition; on and onto are neutral about force. Put the ladder on the wall is odd; lean it against the wall is right, because against supplies the pressure. For a target you aim at but may miss, use at — threw a rock at the window (aim) vs. threw a rock against the window (it landed).
entries.see also: toward, into, onto, at, on

entries.meaning: Names the limit of a movement or an extent: the point where the walking, the driving, or the seeing stops. The literal spatial sense extends easily to abstract reach (as far as the evidence goes). Beware the clause version, which is a completely different animal: as far as I know hedges a statement and has nothing to do with distance.
examples: She walked as far as the mailbox and had to sit down. (1)
The bus goes as far as Ninth Street, then loops back. (1)
Corn as far as the eye could see. (2)
The flood reached as far as the second step. (2)
His authority runs as far as the state line. (3)
The grant covers tuition, but only as far as the first two years. (3)

senses.head: The farthest point of a motion
body: We drove as far as Flagstaff and turned back.

senses.head: The limit of an extent or a view
body: Wheat as far as the horizon.

senses.head: The limit of an abstract reach
body: The rules apply as far as the county line, and no further.
examples: She walked as far as the mailbox and had to sit down. (1)
The bus goes as far as Ninth Street, then loops back. (1)

entries.pronunciation note: uhz-FAR-uhz
entries.русский: до (самого) — крайняя точка движения, протяжённости или охвата
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only. With a clause it stops being a preposition and becomes a conjunction (as far as I know, as far as anyone can tell) — a different construction with a different meaning.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] as far as [noun phrase] · [measurement] as far as [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: As far as marks the far end of a distance actually covered; up to marks a ceiling that may not be reached (up to fifty people means fifty at most). We walked as far as the bridge says the bridge is where we stopped. Note also the disputed truncation as far as money, we're fine — standard edited English wants as far as money is concerned or simply as for money.
entries.see also: up to, to, toward, down to, back to

entries.meaning: The summit preposition. It was built the same way as aboard and ashore — a worn-down on fused to a noun — and it does in one word what on top of does in three, which is exactly why headline writers and sportswriters reach for it. Its figurative life is almost entirely about rankings and hierarchies: a team sits atop the standings, an executive sits atop an organization.
examples: A wind sock hung atop the pole at the end of the runway. (1)
Snow was still sitting atop the ridge in June. (1)
She climbed atop the stepladder to reach the smoke detector. (2)
The cat hauled itself atop the refrigerator and stayed there all afternoon. (2)
They finished the week atop the conference for the first time since 2011. (3)
He spent twelve years atop the agency before anyone questioned the budget. (3)
A second rate hike atop the one in March would break the deal. (4)
The fee sits atop everything else the school already charges. (4)

senses.head: Position on the top of
body: A weather vane atop the barn.

senses.head: Motion to the top of
body: He scrambled atop the boulder.

senses.head: Highest in a ranking or a hierarchy (figurative)
body: They finished the season atop the division.

senses.head: Piled on; added to what is already there
body: Another delay atop the two we already had.

entries.pronunciation note: uh-TAWP in the regions where the cot–caught merger settles on the rounded vowel — the same variation you hear in on, onto, and upon. The vowel is the one in top, so speakers who keep the two apart use /ɑ/ here
entries.русский: на вершине, на верх — сверху чего-то; перен. на первом месте в списке или иерархии
entries.register: neutral to formal; commonest in journalism, sports writing, and physical description
entries.type: compound (a- "on" + top, fused — the same a- that built aboard, ashore, astride, away)
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — no gerunds, no clauses of any kind. It is one of the most restricted prepositions in this file: it wants a concrete object that has a top. Unlike aboard, around, and along, it has no bare adverb use — he stood atop with nothing after it is not English.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] atop [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] atop [noun phrase] · [noun] atop [noun phrase] (the flag atop the dome) · sit / perch / sit atop [noun phrase]
entries.variants: on top of — the ordinary spoken equivalent and the safer choice in plain prose; see on top of. The older a-top of is obsolete.
entries.contrast: Atop is onto and on compressed into one word with a summit added: it asserts that the object has a high point and that the thing is at it. A book on the table is neutral; a book atop the table is faintly odd, because a table's top is not a summit. Reserve it for things with a real high point — a hill, a roof, a pole, a stack, a standings table. Against upon: both are raised in register, but upon is about contact and atop is about height.
entries.see also: onto, upon, on, over, aboard, up

entries.meaning: Return motion — to a place, a state, an activity, or a point in the past. The back carries all the "again" meaning; to supplies the destination. In its temporal sense it reaches from the present into the past, which is why it pairs with date, go, trace, and reach.
examples: We drove back to the hotel in the dark. (1)
He moved back to Ohio after the divorce. (1)
The swelling went back to normal overnight. (2)
After the layoffs, nothing went back to the way it was. (2)
She went back to teaching after ten years in software. (3)
Getting back to your question — no, we haven't decided. (3)
The family's records go back to the 1830s. (4)
The feud traces back to an argument over a fence. (4)

senses.head: Return to a state or condition

senses.head: Return to an activity or topic
body: Let's get back to the schedule.

entries.pronunciation note: BAK-tuh
entries.русский: обратно в/к — возвращение к месту, состоянию, занятию или в прошлое
entries.type: complex (adverb back + preposition to, fixed as a unit)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (back to working nights) — never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] back to [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] back to [noun phrase] · back to [verb-ing] · dates back to [year]
entries.contrast: Plain to is neutral about whether you have been there before; back to asserts you have. Go to Denver is a trip; go back to Denver is a return. Do not confuse the temporal sense (dates back to 1890) with since, which measures forward from a start point rather than reaching backward from now.
entries.see also: to, down to, up to, away from, from

entries.meaning: Motion to a lower place, a farther-along point, or a smaller amount. The "lower" is often social or geographic rather than literal — Americans go down to the city, down to Florida, and down to the store without any change in elevation.
examples: He went down to the basement to reset the breaker. (1)
They drove down to Austin for the weekend. (1)
The doctor got her dosage down to five milligrams. (2)
We cut the guest list down to forty. (2)
The set is period-accurate down to the light switches. (3)
Everything was accounted for down to the last penny. (3)

body: We walked down to the water.

senses.head: Reduction to a level
body: Trim it down to four minutes.

entries.pronunciation note: DOWN-tuh
entries.русский: вниз до; вплоть до — движение к нижней точке; снижение до уровня; включая мелочи
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (came down to choosing between two) — never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] down to [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] down to [noun phrase] · everything down to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Directional down to mirrors up to and, like it, has an "as far as and including" sense — but down to the last detail scans the list from big to small, while up to fifty counts from zero to a ceiling. The British sense "attributable to" (it's down to you, that's down to the weather) is not American; Americans say up to you for responsibility and because of or due to for cause.
entries.see also: down, up to, back to, as far as, to

entries.meaning: The in-transit preposition. English already owns to, toward, and on the way to, but none of them states as flatly that the motion is under way, which is why dispatchers, airlines, and delivery notifications run on this one. Sportswriting then borrowed it for a figurative sense — the points a player scores en route to a win are the ones scored along the way — and that use is now at least as common in American print as the literal one.
examples: The ambulance was en route to the hospital when the call was canceled. (1)
Your package is en route to the sorting facility in Memphis. (1)
Two of the crates were damaged en route to the warehouse. (1)
The delegation stopped in Reykjavik en route to Brussels. (2)
We refueled twice en route to the coast. (2)
He threw for four touchdowns en route to a 38–10 win. (3)
She set a personal best en route to winning her third state title. (3)
The bill picked up nine amendments en route to the governor's desk. (3)

senses.head: Stopping or passing through, on the way somewhere else
body: We spent a night in Amarillo en route to Santa Fe.

body: She broke two records en route to the title.

entries.pronunciation note: en-ROOT-too. Weak /ˌɑn ˈrut tə/ · ahn-ROOT-tuh, with the same to → /tə/ reduction as up to and back to. The route here is /rut/ — ROOT, never the American /raʊt/ ROWT. ✗en ROWT is the pronunciation error to avoid
entries.русский: по пути в/к, следуя в — в дороге к пункту назначения (офиц., книжн.)
entries.register: neutral to formal; standard in travel, shipping, aviation, and news writing
entries.type: complex (three words — the French borrowing en route plus English to)
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun — a destination or an outcome. A gerund is idiomatic in the figurative "on the way to achieving" sense that sportswriting made common (en route to winning her third title), but never a finite clause: en route to he arrived is not English. Strip the to and bare en route is an adverb with no object at all (the parts are en route), which is the test for telling the two uses apart.
entries.pattern: [be / verb of motion] en route to [destination] · [clause], en route to [destination] · en route to [verb-ing] (figurative)
entries.variants: ✗enroute — the closed spelling is common in aviation and military writing and is still treated as an error in edited American prose. Keep the two words.
entries.contrast: En route to insists that the trip has started and has not finished, which is what separates it from plain to and from toward: flying to Denver reports the whole trip, en route to Denver reports only the part in progress. Against via: via names the waypoint and en route to names the destination not yet reached, so the two sit at opposite ends of the same journey and often appear in one sentence (en route to Santa Fe via Amarillo).
entries.see also: to, toward, via, as far as, on to, by way of

entries.meaning: The long form of toward, useful mainly for pointing rather than going. Because it names a bearing and commits to nothing else, it is also the standard hedge in official and political language — nobody who calls a policy a step in the direction of something has promised to arrive. Learners meet it constantly in reading and should recognize it on sight, but should reach for the one-word preposition when writing.
examples: The herd moved slowly in the direction of the river. (1)
He drove off in the direction of the interstate without saying where he was going. (1)
Rescuers headed in the direction of where the last signal came from. (1)
She tipped her chin in the direction of the man by the window. (2)
The trooper pointed in the direction of the exit ramp. (2)
Everyone in the diner turned in the direction of the noise. (2)
The settlement is a small step in the direction of real oversight. (3)
Nothing in the budget moves in the direction of the reforms they promised. (3)

senses.head: Moving on a bearing toward something
body: The smoke drifted in the direction of the highway.

senses.head: Pointing, looking, or gesturing toward, with no motion of the pointer
body: She nodded in the direction of the back office.

senses.head: Partial or hedged progress toward a goal (figurative)
body: The vote is a step in the direction of full repeal.

entries.pronunciation note: in-thuh-duh-REK-shun-uh — the final of reduces to a bare schwa in every ordinary use, exactly as it does in out of and off of. Both /dəˈrɛkʃən/ and /daɪˈrɛkʃən/ are standard American, and the unstressed /də-/ is the commoner one inside this phrase
entries.русский: в направлении, в сторону — по курсу к чему-то, без обещания дойти
entries.register: neutral, but four syllables longer than the word it replaces; in political and official prose it is usually a hedge
entries.type: complex (four words: preposition + determiner + noun + preposition)
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun — the object belongs to the final of. It also takes a nominal wh-clause (in the direction of where the shots came from), which is a noun phrase in disguise; it never takes a that-clause. A gerund is grammatical but graceless (a move in the direction of settling) — write toward settling.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] in the direction of [noun phrase] · point / gesture / nod / look / turn in the direction of [noun phrase] · a step / a move in the direction of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: This is toward in four words, and toward is nearly always the better choice. The phrase earns its length in exactly two places: when the direction is being indicated rather than traveled (he nodded in the direction of the door — he did not move, so toward would mislead), and when a writer wants to name a bearing without claiming a destination (a move in the direction of reform promises less than a move toward reform). Against as far as: that names a limit actually reached; this names a bearing only. If toward fits, use toward.
entries.see also: toward, to, as far as, up to, away from, via

entries.meaning: Not a preposition, but the counterpart the onto / on to pair makes everyone expect — and the error it prevents is funnier and commoner than its sibling's. Two distinct things hide behind the same two words: to as a real preposition after a particle verb (hand it in to the office) and to as an infinitive marker of purpose (stopped in to say hello). Neither can ever be spelled into.
examples: She turned the paperwork in to the registrar on Friday. (particle verb: turn in)
He dropped in to see how the remodel was going. (particle verb: drop in + infinitive)
Log in to the payroll site with your employee number. (particle verb: log in)
They finally gave in to the union's last demand. (particle verb: give in)
I'll come in to sign the forms tomorrow morning. (particle verb: come in + infinitive)
Turn your keys in to the front desk when you check out. (particle verb: turn in)
Compare: she walked into the registrar's office. (true preposition — one word)
entries.pronunciation note: in-tuh
entries.русский: не предлог: частица глагола in + to — «сдал in to», «зашёл in to поговорить»; не into
entries.type: complex (two words) — strictly the adverb/particle in plus the preposition or infinitive marker to, not a preposition in its own right
entries.complement: whatever the following to takes — a noun phrase or objective pronoun when to is a preposition (turned it in to the clerk), or a bare verb when to is the infinitive marker (came in to talk). Never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [verb + in] to [noun phrase] · [verb + in] to [bare verb] · [verb] [object] in to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The mirror image of on to, and the test is the same. If "to a position inside" fits, write into as one word. If in belongs to the verb — turn in, hand in, drop in, come in, stop in, check in, log in, give in, cave in, tune in, sit in, call in — the words stay apart. He turned himself in to the police means he surrendered; he turned himself into the police means he became them.
entries.see also: into, on to, onto, in, to

entries.meaning: The general preposition of entry — motion from outside to inside, with the boundary crossed. The dog bolted into the woods and didn't come back for an hour. (1)
She backed into a pole in the parking garage. (2)
He walked straight into the screen door. (2)
Translate the whole thing into Spanish by Friday. (3)
The argument turned into a shouting match. (3)
We were three weeks into the semester before anyone noticed. (4)
They kept rehearsing into the early morning. (4)
The board opened an investigation into the missing funds. (5)
I'll look into what happened with your order. (5)
He's been into woodworking since he retired. (6)
She's not into horror movies at all. (6)
I ran into my old landlord at the hardware store. (7)
We bumped into each other outside the courthouse. (7)
Four into twenty goes five times. (8)
Divide the class into groups of three. (8)

entries.русский: в (внутрь) — движение внутрь, в отличие от статического in; врезаться в; превратиться в
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, gerund (got into arguing about it), or a wh-clause in the inquiry sense (an investigation into what went wrong, look into how this happened) — never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] into [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] into [noun phrase] · into [wh-clause] · stranded: the room she walked into; what did you get yourself into?
entries.contrast: in is position, into is motion — He was in the pool vs. He jumped into the pool. This is the central contrast of the whole file. Separately, write in to as two words when in belongs to the verb: turned himself in to the police (he surrendered), came in to talk, dropped in to say hi. Turned himself into the police would mean he became them.

entries.meaning: The plain-English in-transit phrase, and one of the highest-frequency multiword prepositions in American speech. Its literal job is to locate something inside a trip that has started and not finished, which is why so much of its work is incidental (grab coffee on the way to the airport). Its figurative sense — partway to an outcome — is where the common advanced error lives, because that to is a preposition and takes a gerund.
examples: Call me when you're on the way to the airport. (1)
The truck broke down on the way to the job site. (1)
We can pick up the cake on the way to your mother's. (2)
There's a hardware store on the way to the trailhead. (2)
The team is well on the way to a losing season. (3)
She's on the way to becoming the youngest partner the firm has had. (3 — gerund complement)
Compare the objectless adverbial: don't worry, the parts are on the way. (no object — not this preposition)

senses.head: In transit to a destination
body: We're on the way to the hospital now.

senses.head: Passed or done during a trip; lying along the route
body: There's a good diner on the way to the lake.

senses.head: Partway to an outcome or a state (figurative)

entries.pronunciation note: uhn-thuh-WAY-tuh — on and the final to both fall to schwa, so the whole phrase is one unstressed run around a single stressed WAY. Casual speech goes further, to /ənə ˈweɪ tə/ · uh-nuh-WAY-tuh
entries.русский: по пути в/к — по дороге к цели, попутно; перен. на пути к результату
entries.register: neutral — the plain-English everyday equivalent of en route to
entries.type: complex (four words: preposition + determiner + noun + preposition)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund in the figurative sense (on the way to becoming a nurse) — never a finite clause: ✗on the way to he arrived. The to here is a preposition, not an infinitive marker, so a verb after it has to be an -ing form: ✗on the way to become a nurse is the error to avoid, the same trap that catches look forward to and object to. Strip the to and bare on the way is an adverbial with no object at all (the parts are on the way), which is the test for telling the two uses apart.
entries.pattern: [be / verb of motion] on the way to [destination] · [clause], on the way to [destination] · on the way to [verb-ing] · [verb] [object] on the way to [destination]
entries.variants: on my / your / his / her / our / their way to — the possessive version is at least as common as the definite article and means the same thing (she called on her way to the airport). On the road to is the same frame with a different noun and is now almost entirely figurative (on the road to recovery).
entries.contrast: On the way to and en route to mean the same thing; en route to is the shorter and more official one, and on the way to is what Americans say out loud. Against plain to: drove to the airport reports the whole trip, while on the way to the airport frames it as a stretch in the middle of one. Against toward: toward names a bearing and promises no destination, while on the way to names the destination and says only that you have not reached it yet.
entries.see also: en route to, to, toward, up to, via, in the direction of

entries.meaning: Not a preposition, but the single most useful non-entry in this file: American writers get onto and on to wrong constantly, and the error is always in the same direction — collapsing a particle verb into a false preposition. Read the sentence with on attached to the verb; if it still makes sense, the words stay apart. One genuine gray area: be on to someone ("have discovered what they're doing") is written both ways in edited American prose, with onto now slightly commoner.
examples: Hold on to the handrail — those steps are slick. (particle verb: hold on)
Let's move on to the second item. (particle verb: move on)
She passed the message on to her supervisor. (particle verb: pass on)
Log on to the portal with your employee ID. (particle verb: log on)
Hang on to that receipt in case it doesn't fit. (particle verb: hang on)
He signed on to the project in March. (particle verb: sign on)
Compare: she stepped onto the platform. (true preposition — one word)
entries.pronunciation note: AHN-tuh
entries.русский: не предлог: частица глагола on + to — «держаться on to», «перейти on to»; не onto
entries.type: complex (two words) — strictly the adverb/particle on plus the preposition to, not a preposition in its own right
entries.complement: whatever to takes — noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (moved on to fixing the roof) — never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [verb + on] to [noun phrase] · hold on to [noun phrase] · pass [object] on to [noun phrase] · move on to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The whole entry exists for one test. If you can substitute "to a position on top of," write onto as one word. If on belongs to the verb — hold on, move on, pass on, hang on, sign on, log on, catch on — keep the two words apart. He held on to the rail (he gripped it) vs. He climbed onto the rail (he got up on it). Log on to the server, not log onto the server.
entries.see also: onto, in to, into, on, to, up to

entries.meaning: The surface counterpart of into: motion that ends with the moving thing resting on a surface. The extension to data and media (copy it onto a drive) treats the destination as a surface, and the informal "aware of" sense treats a person's scheme as something you have climbed on top of.
examples: She stepped onto the platform just as the doors closed. (1)
The cat leapt onto the counter the second we left. (1)
Load the boxes onto the truck first. (2)
He transferred the tape onto his laptop. (2)
Their balcony looks onto the parking lot. (3)
The kitchen door opens onto the alley. (3)
I think she's onto something with that theory. (4)
Don't bother lying — they've been onto you for weeks. (4)

entries.contrast: on is position, onto is motion — The cat was on the roof vs. The cat jumped onto the roof. And see on to for the two-word spelling: use onto only where "to a position on top of" fits.
entries.see also: on, on to, into, off, upon, over

entries.meaning: Direction without commitment to arrival — which makes it the preposition of aim, orientation, approach, and partial progress. Its abstract senses all preserve that logic: an attitude toward something faces it, money toward a purchase moves you closer without completing it, and toward evening approaches evening without being it.
examples: The herd drifted toward the far fence. (1)
We rowed toward the lights on shore. (1)
He tilted the lamp toward the page. (2)
All the seats face toward the stage. (2)
It usually clouds over toward evening. (3)
Toward the end of the book she loses the thread. (3)
Her policy toward latecomers is not forgiving. (4)
Public opinion has shifted toward the proposal. (4)
That's a real step toward fixing the problem. (5)
Half his paycheck went toward the loan. (5)

entries.pronunciation note: one syllable); also /təˈwɔrd/ · tuh-WORD, /ˈtoʊərd/ · TOH-erd. The one-syllable /tɔrd/ is itself the reduced form — it is what Americans say in ordinary connected speech, and the two-syllable /təˈwɔrd/ is the careful or emphatic pronunciation, not the other way around. The -s of towards does not change any of this
entries.русский: к, по направлению к — направление, обращённость, приближение во времени, отношение к кому-то
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (a step toward solving it) — never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] toward [noun phrase] · [noun] toward [noun phrase] (his attitude toward the job) · toward [verb-ing]
entries.variants: towards — identical in meaning. American English strongly prefers toward; towards is the dominant British form. Both are correct in the United States; pick one and be consistent within a document. The same -s alternation runs through forward(s), backward(s), upward(s), afterward(s).
entries.contrast: to arrives; toward only aims. She ran to the door means she got there; she ran toward the door leaves it open. That is the whole difference and it is reliable. Against at: threw it at me is aggressive and targeted, threw it toward me is merely directional.
entries.see also: to, at, into, up to, away from, as far as

entries.meaning: The King James Bible preserved unto long after ordinary English dropped it, which is why it survives almost entirely in quotation and in a handful of frozen idioms. It is worth knowing because Americans encounter it constantly in hymns, oaths, older legal boilerplate, and the phrases a law unto himself and do unto others.
examples: "Suffer the little children to come unto me." (1)
He rendered unto the county what the county was owed. (1)
She stayed loyal unto the very end. (2)
They swore to defend it unto the last man. (2)
The coach is a law unto himself and the athletic director knows it. (3)
Do unto others as you would have them do unto you. (3)

senses.head: To (motion or recipient) — archaic
body: Come unto me.

senses.head: Until, up to the point of — archaic
body: Faithful unto death.

senses.head: Fixed modern idioms
body: He is a law unto himself.
examples: "Suffer the little children to come unto me." (1)
He rendered unto the county what the county was owed. (1)
She stayed loyal unto the very end. (2)

entries.pronunciation note: UN-tuh
entries.русский: устар., библ. к, до — стилизованная замена to; в живой речи только в застывших оборотах
entries.type: compound (un- + to, on the model of until)
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — no gerunds, no clauses.
entries.pattern: [verb] unto [noun phrase] · [noun] unto [noun phrase] (a law unto himself)
entries.contrast: In every living use, unto is a stylistically marked substitute for to. Using it in ordinary modern prose reads as either scriptural pastiche or unintentional comedy — the sole exceptions are the three fixed phrases below.
entries.see also: to, upon, toward, up to

entries.meaning: Motion as far as a point — and then, by an easy extension, a maximum, a standard, a capability, and an obligation. The "doing something (usually shady)" sense is one of the most idiomatic constructions in casual American English and has no literal spatial content left in it.
examples: A stranger came up to me outside the station. (1)
He drove up to the gate and rolled down the window. (1)
The theater seats up to four hundred. (2)
Delivery takes up to ten business days. (2)
Up to that point the meeting had gone fine. (3)
She'd been sober up to the wedding. (3)
I'm not up to going out tonight. (4)
Is he really up to the job? (4)
The kids have been suspiciously quiet — they're up to something. (5)
What have you been up to since graduation? (5)
Whether we appeal is up to the client. (6)
It's up to you where we eat. (6)
The inspector said the deck isn't up to code. (7)
His second album wasn't up to the first. (7)

senses.head: Doing something, usually mischief

senses.head: Someone's decision or responsibility
body: It's up to the committee now.

senses.head: Meeting a standard
body: The wiring isn't up to code.

entries.pronunciation note: UP-tuh
entries.русский: до, вплоть до — предел; разг. «замышлять что-то», «дело за кем-то», «быть в состоянии»
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (not up to driving tonight); a wh-clause only in the "someone's choice" sense with extraposition (it's up to you how we split it). Never a bare that-clause.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] up to [noun phrase] · up to [number] · be up to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · it's up to [pronoun] · stranded: what are you up to?
entries.contrast: Up to names a ceiling that may not be reached (up to fifty people = fifty at most, possibly fewer); as far as names a limit actually reached. Against down to: both mean "as far as and including," but up to counts upward from nothing and down to scans from large to small.
entries.see also: up, down to, as far as, to, on to

entries.meaning: The elevated twin of on, and — in its motion sense — a near-synonym of onto with a sudden or forceful edge: things fall upon, descend upon, and come upon one another. Its most genuinely useful modern job is temporal: upon arrival and upon signing compress a whole clause into two words, which is why contracts and instructions are full of it.
examples: A heavy snow lay upon the fields. (1)
The inscription upon the stone had worn away. (1)
Winter descended upon the valley all at once. (2)
The crowd surged upon the barricades. (2)
Upon signing, you'll receive a copy of the agreement. (3)
Upon hearing the verdict, she left without a word. (3)
I happened upon the letter while cleaning out the attic. (4)
They stumbled upon the wreck by accident. (4)
Mile upon mile of the same brown grass. (5)
Thousands upon thousands of people showed up. (5)

entries.pronunciation note: uh-PAWN. The first syllable is already reduced and there is no further weak form: it is /ə/, never the full /ʌp/ of up, and ✗UP-on is the commonest mispronunciation among learners who see the spelling before they hear the word
entries.русский: на — книжн. вариант on; также «сразу после (чего-то)» и «наткнуться на»
entries.register: formal, literary, or fixed-phrase; in plain modern prose on is the default
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (upon signing the contract) — never a finite clause. The gerund pattern is the one place upon beats on in modern American writing.
entries.pattern: [verb] upon [noun phrase] · Upon [noun phrase / verb-ing], [main clause] · [noun] upon [same noun] (row upon row)
entries.contrast: Upon and on mean the same thing; upon is longer, heavier, and more formal. Reaching for it to sound elegant is the classic overcorrection — sit upon the couch is simply worse than sit on the couch. Reserve it for the four places it earns its keep: after certain verbs (depend upon, call upon, seize upon), in the temporal upon + gerund, in the doubling pattern (row upon row), and in frozen phrases (once upon a time).
entries.see also: on, onto, over, unto, up

entries.meaning: The direct opposite of toward: motion whose whole point is that the gap is widening. It also does static duty as a distance measurement, and it carries a strong secondary sense of deliberate avoidance, which is why warnings use it (stay away from the edge).
examples: He backed slowly away from the dog. (1)
The plane banked away from the ridge. (1)
The cabin is four miles away from the nearest road. (2)
They live two doors away from my parents. (2)
The company is shifting away from hardware entirely. (3)
She's been drifting away from her old friends. (3)
Keep the kids away from the fireworks. (4)
I'd stay away from that restaurant if I were you. (4)

senses.head: Motion increasing distance
body: The boat pulled away from the dock.

senses.head: Distance measured from a point (static)
body: We're twenty minutes away from the airport.

senses.head: Abstract shift or change of course
body: The industry is moving away from coal.

entries.pronunciation note: uh-WAY-fruhm
entries.русский: от, прочь от — удаление от точки; на расстоянии от; перен. уход от чего-то, избегание
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (moving away from using coal) — never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] away from [noun phrase] · [measurement] away from [noun phrase] (two blocks away from the station) · away from [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Plain from names the origin of a trip (flew from Denver); away from stresses increasing distance and often avoidance (flew away from the storm). Against out of: out of requires an enclosure to exit, away from does not — you move away from a tree, never out of one.
entries.see also: from, toward, out of, off, past

entries.meaning: The safe-distance preposition. The adjective clear — "unobstructed, free" — hardened onto of and now works as a single unit, with one idea running through all of it: something dangerous, obstructing, or entangling has been left far enough behind to stop counting. That is why controllers, dispatchers, and safety notices are built on the phrase, and why its commonest everyday shape is a warning rather than a report.
examples: The ferry swung clear of the barge with about a yard to spare. (1)
He dragged the mower clear of the burning shed. (1)
Wait until the truck is clear of the crosswalk before you turn. (2)
The scaffolding has to stay eight feet clear of the power line. (2)
By March the company was finally clear of the receivership. (3)
He never got clear of the rumor, even after the charges were dropped. (3)
Stay clear of the tracks until the gates go back up. (4)
My advice is to steer clear of asking him about the sale. (4 — gerund complement)

body: The tug pulled clear of the pilings.

senses.head: At a safe distance from; no longer touching or threatened by
body: The wingtip was barely clear of the hangar door.

senses.head: Free of an entanglement, a debt, or a suspicion (figurative)
body: Two more payments and she'll be clear of the loan.

senses.head: Deliberately avoiding, with steer, stay, or keep
body: Steer clear of that intersection at five o'clock.
examples: The ferry swung clear of the barge with about a yard to spare. (1)
He dragged the mower clear of the burning shed. (1)

entries.pronunciation note: KLEER-uh — the of drops to a bare schwa in every ordinary use, exactly as it does in out of and off of. The stress never leaves clear, and ✗kleer-UV is the mistake to avoid
entries.русский: в стороне от, подальше от — на безопасном расстоянии; свободный от долга или подозрения
entries.register: neutral; standard in aviation, maritime, traffic, and safety writing, and in the everyday warning steer clear of
entries.type: complex (the adjective clear + of, fixed as a unit)
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund in the avoidance sense (steer clear of asking him about it) — never a finite clause: ✗clear of he was involved. The to-infinitive is impossible here, because the of is a preposition: ✗steer clear of to ask him and ✗steer clear of ask him are both wrong, and only steer clear of asking him is English. With no object at all, clear is an adjective or an adverb (the runway is clear, she got clear), which is the test for telling the two uses apart.
entries.pattern: steer / stay / keep clear of [noun phrase] · [verb of motion] clear of [noun phrase] (pull, swing, haul, get clear of) · be clear of [noun phrase] · clear of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Against away from: away from says only that the gap is widening, while clear of says a specific hazard has been escaped completely — the plane banked away from the ridge reports the motion, the plane was clear of the ridge reports that the ridge no longer mattered. Against out of: out of needs an enclosure to exit, clear of needs only something to be obstructed or endangered by. Against past: past the barge is merely beyond it; clear of the barge is far enough beyond it to be safe.
entries.see also: away from, out of, past, off, out from under, of

entries.meaning: Two senses that share a spelling and almost nothing else. The spatial stack is old and formal — a waiter clears a plate from before a guest, a figure rises from before a fire — and it survives mostly in literary description and in the reporting of ceremony. The temporal one is everyday American English and means simply "dating from earlier than": a photo from before the fire, records from before the merger. Only context separates them, which is why the spatial use needs a physical verb around it to be readable at all.
examples: The dog had to be coaxed from before the oven door. (1)
The guard stepped from before the gate and waved them through. (1)
A waiter cleared the cups from before the two of them without a word. (2)
He pulled the microphone from before her face. (2)
Everything in the album is from before the divorce. (3)
She still has letters from before the family left Poland. (3)
Compare the clause version, where before is a conjunction: I've known him from before he moved to Denver. (not this preposition)

senses.head: Away from a position in front of something
body: He rose from before the hearth.

senses.head: Taking something out of the space in front of a person
body: She lifted the untouched plate from before him.

senses.head: Dating from a time earlier than
body: A photograph from before the fire.
examples: The dog had to be coaxed from before the oven door. (1)
The guard stepped from before the gate and waved them through. (1)
A waiter cleared the cups from before the two of them without a word. (2)
He pulled the microphone from before her face. (2)
Everything in the album is from before the divorce. (3)
She still has letters from before the family left Poland. (3)
Compare the clause version, where before is a conjunction: I've known him from before he moved to Denver. (not this preposition)

entries.pronunciation note: fruhm-buh-FOR — both words reduce, so in running speech the phrase is two schwas leading into the stressed -FOR. From is never stressed here unless the source is being contrasted with some other source
entries.русский: книжн. из пространства перед чем-то; о времени — «ещё до», «с времён до чего-то»
entries.register: the spatial sense is formal, literary, and rare; the temporal sense (from before the war) is neutral and completely ordinary in American speech
entries.type: complex (a preposition stack: from + before in its "in front of" sense)
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun — the object belongs to before. A gerund is marginal (from before joining the firm) and reads badly; rewrite with a noun (from before her time at the firm). With a finite clause the before stops being a preposition and becomes a conjunction — I've known him from before he moved here is good English, but there from governs a whole subordinate clause, which is a different construction from from before the war.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] from before [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] from before [person] · [noun] from before [period] · rise / step / clear / snatch from before [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The spatial sense is built exactly like out from under and like from behind: a position preposition with from stacked on the front to mark that position as the source. Against plain from: took it from him makes the person the source, took it from before him makes the space in front of him the source. American writers use the spatial sense sparingly, because readers hear the temporal before first and have to back up. For the temporal preposition on its own see before (time); for the spatial one see before (place).
entries.see also: from, before (place), before (time), out from under, away from, from off

entries.meaning: A preposition stack that standard American English has retired. It was ordinary in Early Modern English, and the King James Bible preserved it — I will destroy it from off the face of the earth, wipe away tears from off all faces — which is why it still reads as scripture rather than as merely old. It also survives as living regional speech in parts of the South and Appalachia, where it carries no archaic flavor whatever. Recognize it in reading and in dialogue; in your own writing use off.
examples: The stone was rolled from off the mouth of the tomb. (1 — biblical register)
The promise is that every tear will be wiped from off their faces. (1 — biblical register)

entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — the object belongs to off. No gerunds and no clauses of any kind: ✗from off he left it there. Neither half can be stranded on its own; the stack moves as a unit.

entries.meaning: Two related stacks with quite different lives. Bare from out belongs to poetry and nineteenth-century prose (from out the shadows, from out the depths), and reaching for it today is a deliberate effect that reads as pastiche if it misses. From out of is not archaic in the least; it is everyday spoken American English, where the doubled source marking adds emphasis. Both get cut in edited writing, and both are worth recognizing on sight.
examples: A single light showed from out the fog. (1)
A cry came from out the depths of the canyon. (1)
She fished the spare key from out of the flowerpot. (2)
He dragged the box from out of the crawl space. (2)
A dog appeared from out of the corn and sat down in the road. (3)
The offer came from out of nowhere three days before the deadline. (3)
Edited prose deletes the from in every one of these. (register note)

entries.meaning: The redundant doublet of off. entries.meaning: One of the few genuinely productive preposition stacks left in English, and American English treats it as a single unit. The literal sense is the exit of something covered or pinned — a cat out from under a parked truck, a foot out from under a fallen beam. The figurative sense generalizes the weight to anything that presses down: a debt, a boss, a contract, a verdict.
examples: The cat shot out from under the parked truck when the engine started. (1)
She wriggled out from under the collapsed shelving without a scratch. (1)
He backed the mower out from under the deck stairs. (2)
Somebody yanked the rug out from under the whole argument. (2)
Two more payments and they'll be out from under the second mortgage. (3)
The division never got out from under the last reorganization. (3)
It took a decade to climb out from under that verdict. (3)

entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — the object belongs to under. No gerunds, no clauses of any kind: write out from under the mortgage, never out from under he owed money. Unlike out and under on their own, the stack has no bare adverb use — he finally got out from under with nothing after it is heard in speech but leaves the object to be understood, not deleted.

Against out of: out of needs an enclosure, out from under needs only something on top. Against off: off leaves a surface you were on, out from under leaves a weight you were beneath.

entries.meaning: A regional American form of out of, listed here so readers can identify it and writers know to leave it alone. Where it lives it is ordinary speech and carries no stigma; outside those areas — in edited prose, or in a classroom — it will be read as an error, and the honest advice is to recognize it and write out of. It is included for the same reason athwart is: you will meet it in reading, not because anyone should reach for it.

Get outen my kitchen with those boots on. (1)
She drank the water right outen the dipper. (1)
The handle was whittled outen a piece of hickory. (2)
Nothing good ever came outen that hollow, he told us. (2)
Standard American English writes every one of these with out of. (register note)

entries.meaning: Motion from one edge of a surface to the opposite edge. Once the crossing is complete, the same word names the resulting position (the diner across the street), and once you stop thinking of a single line, it names distribution over a whole area (offices across the country). Across has the usual second life outside this word class: an adverb with no object (she waved and ran across) and a verb particle in two very common phrasal verbs, come across (encounter, or make an impression) and get across (communicate). The object test settles which is which — swam across the river has an object and is the preposition, swam across to the far bank has none and is the adverb, and in the point never got across the word belongs to the verb.
examples: She ran across the field to catch up. (1)
We drove across three states in a day. (1)
He lives across the hall from me. (2)
There's a bakery across the square. (2)
The company has offices across the country. (3)
Reaction was mixed across the department. (3)
A fallen pine lay across the driveway. (4)
She drew a line across the page. (4)

entries.contrast: The three-way traversal contrast is the one to memorize. Across is a two-dimensional surface, side to side (swam across the river); through is a three-dimensional medium you are inside of (waded through the river); over is above an obstacle, or across a raised surface (jumped over the puddle, drove over the bridge). All three can describe the same river; they describe different trips.

entries.meaning: Motion that follows the length of something linear, or position strung out over that length. Because it needs a line to follow, it is the natural preposition for roads, rivers, shorelines, fences, and walls, and it is wrong with an area. It is also a heavily used adverb and particle (come along, bring it along, play along, get along), where it takes no object at all.
examples: She jogged along the canal every morning. (1)
The train runs along the river for twenty miles. (1)
We drove along the coast road until the pavement gave out. (1)
There are streetlights along the whole stretch. (2)
Wildflowers grow along the fence line. (2)
Sandbags were stacked along the levee for half a mile. (2)
He wants something along the lines of what we did last year. (3)
The reforms proceeded along familiar lines. (3)

entries.meaning: The nautical word that came ashore. A ship comes alongside a pier — parallel to it, touching or nearly touching — and every later sense keeps that picture: two things side by side, pointed the same way, one of them usually having moved to get there. The collaboration sense is now the commonest one in American writing, and its deliberate weakness compared with with is the whole reason it gets chosen.
examples: A pickup pulled alongside us and honked. (1)
The tug came alongside the barge and made fast. (1)

entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun, and a gerund in the "in addition to" sense (alongside running the shop, she does the books) — never a finite clause. Write alongside the claim that he lied, never alongside he lied. It is also a bare adverb with no object at all (the tug came alongside, she stayed alongside the whole way), which is the usual test for telling the two uses apart.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] alongside [noun phrase] · [noun] alongside [noun phrase] · work / serve / fight / run alongside [person] · pull / come alongside [vessel or vehicle] · alongside [verb-ing]

entries.contrast: Along follows the length of a line; alongside puts you next to that line, facing the same way. Against beside (a static location preposition): beside is pure position, while alongside keeps the motion and the shared heading of along — she sat beside him is still, the cruiser pulled alongside us is not. Against with for collaboration: worked with the union claims joint action, worked alongside the union claims only proximity and parallel effort, which is precisely why negotiators and press releases reach for it.

entries.meaning: One of the most polysemous prepositions in the language, unified by the idea of a curved or enclosing path. From a circular route it moves to enclosure, to skirting an obstacle, to aimless wandering inside an area, and finally — because a circle has no exact edge — to approximation. It is just as busy outside this word class, as an adverb (turn around, stick around, is she around?) and as a verb particle (mess around, shop around, pass it around), and in both of those jobs it takes no object at all. The object test separates them cleanly: we walked around the block is the preposition, with the block as its object, while we walked around for an hour is the adverb, with nothing after it. The same split holds for the variant: come round is the adverb, round the clock is the preposition.
examples: The trail loops around the lake and comes back. (1)
She wrapped a scarf around her neck. (1)
There's a fence around the whole property. (2)
The kids gathered around the fire pit. (2)
Traffic was routed around the construction. (3)
The bathroom is around the corner on your left. (3)
He spent the afternoon poking around the hardware store. (4)
She showed us around the house. (4)
There were around fifty people at the service. (5)
Let's say around four o'clock. (5)

entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund in the abstract "centered on" sense (built around getting the timing right). Never a finite clause.

entries.variants: round — the same word with the a- worn off. In American English round as a general preposition is British-sounding (walked round the lake); Americans keep it only in fixed expressions: round the clock, all year round, year-round, come round, round about. entries.contrast: Against past: drove around the accident means you took a curving path avoiding it; drove past the accident means you went by in a straight line. entries.meaning: An old crosswise word, one of the a- family built by fusing a worn-down preposition onto a noun. Modern American English keeps it alive mainly as an adverb or a predicate adjective; the prepositional use covered here has retreated to poetry, nature writing, and deliberately heightened description. Most readers have met it in a single line of Shakespeare — the willow that grows aslant a brook in Hamlet — and that is roughly the register it still occupies.
examples: Late light lay aslant the kitchen floor. (1)
Rain drove aslant the windshield the whole way over the pass. (1)
A ladder stood aslant the barn wall, one foot in the mud. (1)
In Hamlet the willow grows aslant a brook, which is where most readers meet the word. (2)
A fallen cottonwood lay aslant the creek and we crossed on it. (2)
Her account runs aslant everything the report concluded. (3)

entries.pronunciation note: the first syllable is already the reduced /ə/ and the stress never leaves -slant, which holds for the whole a- family in this file (aboard, atop, across, along, astride, athwart)
entries.русский: книжн., поэт. наискось через — по диагонали поверх чего-то
entries.register: literary and poetic, and archaic outside verse and heightened description; rare in ordinary American prose
entries.type: compound (a- "on" + slant, fused — the same a- that built aboard, atop, and astride)
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — no gerunds, no clauses of any kind: ✗aslant the roof was leaking. With no object it is an adverb or a predicate adjective (the blind hangs aslant, her hat sat aslant), and that objectless use is in fact its commoner modern life, so the object test matters more here than the word's frequency would suggest.

entries.contrast: Aslant and athwart are the two crosswise words in this file and both are literary; the difference is the angle and the intent. Athwart crosses squarely and usually obstructs, while aslant crosses on a diagonal and usually does not. Against across: across is the ordinary modern word and says nothing about angle, which is why it is almost always the better choice. Against along: along follows a line, aslant cuts one obliquely. In plain American prose write across or at an angle across.

entries.meaning: The straddling preposition — one leg on each side, and by extension one part on each side. It stays alive in ordinary American English for riding (astride a horse, astride the fence) and in a productive figurative use for anything that sits on both sides of a line: a company astride two industries, a town astride a state border.
examples: He climbed astride the fence rail and refused to come down. (1)
The boy sat astride his father's shoulders for the whole parade. (1)
The county road runs astride the ridge for two miles. (2)
Their property lies astride the creek, which is why the survey took so long. (2)
The city is astride the state line and has two of everything. (3)
The company sits astride logistics and retail and answers to regulators in both. (3)

entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — no gerunds, no clauses. It also has a bare adverb use in older prose (he rode astride rather than sidesaddle), but the preposition is what you meet in modern American writing, and it always has an object.

entries.meaning: An old word for "crosswise," surviving chiefly in sailing (athwart the deck, athwartships) and in one famous rhetorical formula — to stand athwart history, yelling Stop. entries.meaning: The far-side preposition. Where past reports the crossing, beyond describes the territory on the other side, which is why it leans literary and why so much of its use has gone figurative: a limit, a capacity, an authority, or an understanding is a boundary you can be on the wrong side of, and beyond is the word that puts you there.

entries.type: compound (be- + yond, the old word for "that place over there")
entries.never a finite clause: write beyond the fact that he was there, never beyond he was there. Beyond is also a bare adverb (the fields beyond) and a noun (the great beyond); as always, the object is the test.
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun; a gerund only in a closed set of "past the point of" idioms (beyond caring, beyond saving, beyond repairing) — you cannot invent new ones.

entries.contrast: Against past, its plainer twin: both put a line behind you, but past is the ordinary word for the motion (drove past the mill) and beyond is the literary word for what lies on the far side (the country beyond the mill). Against over: over the hill passes above it, beyond the hill is on its far side. Against outside for limits: beyond my control and outside my control both work, with beyond the more emphatic and the more final. entries.meaning: Motion from a higher point to a lower one along a path — and then, with the vertical sense bleached out, plain motion along a horizontal path. Americans go down the hall, down the street, and down to the store with no change in elevation. Its two figurative senses run in exact parallel with up: an order travels down the chain of command as readily as a complaint works its way up it, and a decision pushed down the road is postponed rather than lowered. It is equally at home as an adverb and particle (sit down, the system is down, turn it down), and there the object test applies: ran down the hill has an object, the car broke down does not.

Water was running down the inside of the wall. (1)
Walk down Third Street until you hit the light. (2)
The copier is down the corridor on the right. (2)
We paddled down the Green for three days. (3)
The fog moved down the coast overnight. (3)
The recipe has come down the family since her great-grandmother. (4 — literary)
Down the years the town has barely changed. (4 — literary)
We'll worry about the second phase down the road. (4 — everyday)
Three owners down the line, nobody could find the original deed. (4 — everyday)
The order came down the chain of command without a signature on it. (5)
Her name slid down the depth chart after the second injury. (5)

entries.meaning: Along with into, the widest-ranging preposition in this file. The core is a curved path passing above something; from there it spreads to covering, to superiority, to exceeding a number, to spanning a period, and to the topic of a dispute — a chain that makes sense once you see that all of them involve one thing positioned above or beyond another. Over also has a heavy second life outside this word class. It is an adverb (come over, move over, the plane flew over), a verb particle (hand over the keys, turn it over, think it over, start over), and a predicate adjective meaning finished (the meeting is over, it's over between them). Two tests separate them. The object test: he climbed over the fence has an object, the fence fell over does not. The movement test for particles: handed over the keys can be split (handed the keys over), while a true preposition can never be pulled away from its object — ✗climbed the fence over.

entries.meaning: Motion that goes beyond a point without stopping, and then position beyond that point. The clock sense (quarter past four) is the same beyond-ness applied to time, and the abstract sense — past his prime, past caring — applies it to a limit or a capacity. Past is unusually busy outside this word class: an adjective (past events, the past-due balance), a noun (in the past, she has a past), and an adverb with no object at all (a truck rumbled past). The object test matters more here than almost anywhere else in the file, because the adverb and the preposition sit in the same slot after the same verbs: she walked past the diner has an object and is the preposition; she walked past without looking up has none and is the adverb. The adverb is also the form stranded at the end of a relative clause (the store we drove past), where the object has moved to the front rather than disappeared.

He shoved past us to get to the door. (1)
The trailhead is a quarter mile past the bridge. (2)
Their place is just past the grain silo. (2)
The meeting started at half past two. (3)
It was already twenty past by the time she called. (3)
Honestly, I'm past caring what he thinks. (4)
The car is well past the point of being worth fixing. (4)

entries.pattern: [verb of motion] past [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] past [noun phrase] · [minutes] past [hour] · be past [verb-ing] · stranded: the store we drove past
entries.contrast: The spelling trap: past is the preposition, passed is the past tense of the verb pass. We drove past the school and We passed the school are both correct; We drove passed the school is not. If a form of have or be could precede it, or if it is the main verb, you want passed. Against by: drove by the house and drove past the house are near-identical, with past slightly stronger on the idea of going beyond. Against through and around: past skirts the thing entirely without entering or circling it.
entries.see also: by, through, around, across, over, away from

entries.meaning: Motion entering one side of a volume and exiting the other, or moving within a medium. Everything else follows from that: a period of time is a stretch you pass through, a process is something you come out the far side of, and an intermediary is what your action travels through. The inclusive date sense is one of the few places where American and British usage genuinely diverge in meaning rather than style. Outside this word class, through is an adverb (let me through, the bullet went straight through), a verb particle (the deal fell through, read it through, see it through, follow through), and — in sense 6 — a predicate adjective (we're through, are you through?). The object test applies as usual: we drove through the tunnel has an object, the call didn't go through does not.
examples: We walked through the tunnel with a flashlight. (1)
Rain was coming through a gap in the roof. (1)
She waded through knee-deep water to reach the truck. (2)
The plow cut through two feet of drift. (2)
He sat through three hours of testimony. (3)
They got through the audit without a single finding. (3)
The grant came through the state, not the city. (4)
You learn that kind of thing through experience. (4)
The pool is open Memorial Day through Labor Day. (5)
Applications are accepted Monday through Thursday. (5)
I'm through with the whole argument. (6)
Let me know when you're through with the car. (6)

entries.pronunciation note: thruh in rapid speech before a consonant (through the door)
entries.русский: через, сквозь — насквозь; на протяжении всего периода; посредством; амер. «по … включительно»
entries.complement: noun phrase, objective pronoun, or gerund (got through cleaning the garage) — never a finite clause.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] through [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] through [noun phrase] · [day] through [day] · stranded: the tunnel we came through
entries.variants: thru — a respelling, not a separate word. It is acceptable only in signage and trade names (drive-thru, thruway) and in informal notes; in any edited prose it is an error.
entries.contrast: See the three-way traversal rule under across: through means you were inside the thing. Also note a distinctively American use: inclusive through in date ranges — Monday through Friday includes Friday. British English does not use it this way and says Monday to Friday or up to and including Friday, which is why May through September can confuse an international reader. Against by for means: found it through a friend (the friend was the channel) vs. written by a friend (the friend was the agent).
entries.see also: across, over, into, throughout, via, past, by

entries.meaning: Complete penetration of a space, a period, or a population — "in every part of," never "along a route." Its two senses, spatial and temporal, are the same idea applied to extent in space and extent in time. It also works as an adverb with no object (the house was rewired throughout), which is the usual test for separating the two.
examples: Speakers were installed throughout the building. (1)
The blight has turned up throughout the county. (1)
He stayed calm throughout the interview. (2)
Throughout the 1970s the plant ran three shifts. (2)
The error appears throughout the dataset. (3)
Support for the measure was strong throughout the district. (3)

senses.head: In or to every part of a space
body: The smell of paint spread throughout the house.

senses.head: For the whole of a period
body: It rained throughout the night.

senses.head: Among every part of a group or a body of work
body: The same motif recurs throughout her novels.

entries.pronunciation note: thruh-OWT — the stress sits on the second syllable, so the first reduces in connected speech
entries.русский: по всему, на протяжении всего — в каждой части пространства, периода или группы
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — no gerunds, no clauses. It needs an object with extent: a space, a period, or a group. Throughout the box is odd; throughout the building is right.
entries.pattern: [verb] throughout [noun phrase of space or time] · Throughout [noun phrase], [main clause]
entries.contrast: Through traces a path from one end to the other; throughout saturates every part with no path implied. The smoke went through the house describes a route; smoke spread throughout the house describes total coverage. Against during: during the war locates an event inside a period, throughout the war insists it lasted the whole of it.
entries.see also: through, across, over, around, in

entries.meaning: Motion to or position in a place lower than something, usually with the upper thing covering or spanning it. The abstract senses all preserve a sense of being subordinate to something above: less than a number, subject to an authority, or in the middle of a process that is being applied to you. Under is also a bare adverb with no object (the swimmer went under, the business went under) and a productive prefix (underpaid, understaffed, underestimate). It is only a marginal verb particle, though — unlike up, down, over, off, and out, it does not build many phrasal verbs — so the preposition is what you meet nearly every time, and the object test rarely has to work hard: the ball rolled under the couch has an object, the ship rolled and went under does not.
examples: She ducked under the low doorway. (1)
The kayak slid under the footbridge. (1)
There's a box of photos under the stairs. (2)
The keys were under a stack of mail. (2)
The car sat all winter under a tarp. (3)
Half the driveway was under snow. (3)
Kids under twelve get in free. (4)
He ran it in under four hours. (4)
He testified under oath. (5)
Under the new rules, that's no longer allowed. (5)
The proposal is still under review. (6)
Two of the exhibits are under construction. (6)
File the receipts under "travel." (7)
Her earlier books were published under a pen name. (7)

entries.pronunciation note: UN-ner, with the d dropped after the nasal in rapid speech (under the bed)
entries.русский: под — под чем-то; меньше (числа, возраста); под властью или по условиям; в процессе чего-то
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — no gerunds, no clauses. Write under the assumption that he'd agree, never under he'd agree.
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] under [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] under [noun phrase] · under [number] · stranded: the bed it rolled under
entries.contrast: Under is the everyday word and the only one of the four that comfortably takes motion (swam under the bridge). Below is about level on a scale or a vertical position, often at a distance (below sea level, the apartment below). Beneath is under with a formal or literary register, plus the figurative "unworthy of" sense (beneath contempt). Underneath stresses being covered or hidden and is often an adverb (the note was underneath). Against over: they are a true opposite pair across most of their senses.
entries.see also: over, up, down, through, on

entries.meaning: Motion from a lower point to a higher one along a path, or simply motion along a path with the vertical sense worn away. In American usage up also carries a directional charge from regional geography — up north, up the coast, upstate — that has more to do with maps than with elevation. As an adverb and particle it is one of the most frequent words in English (wake up, give up, look it up, use it up), and there it takes no object.
examples: She carried the boxes up the stairs two at a time. (1)
Ivy had grown up the whole north wall. (1)
Go up Fourth Street and take a left at the diner. (2)
The restrooms are up the hall past the elevators. (2)
We poled the boat up the creek as far as it would go. (3)
The barges work their way up the Mississippi in convoys. (3)
Their cabin is about an hour up the lake from the landing. (4)
Everything up the coast from Newport was fogged in. (4)
Word of the defect finally worked its way up the org chart. (5)
She moved up the waiting list after two people dropped out. (5)

entries.pronunciation note: the vowel is already lax and does not reduce further, which is why in up to only the second word weakens (UP-tuh, never uh-TOO)
entries.русский: вверх по — снизу вверх вдоль чего-то; против течения; но также просто «по (улице)», без вертикали
entries.complement: noun phrase or objective pronoun only — no gerunds, no clauses. (The look-alike up to does take a gerund; see up to.)
entries.pattern: [verb of motion] up [noun phrase] · [verb] [object] up [noun phrase] · stranded: the hill we ran up
entries.contrast: The mirror of down, with the same caveat: with vertical objects the two are genuine opposites (up the ladder / down the ladder), but with streets and hallways both mean "along," and Americans use them almost interchangeably (up the street, down the street). Do not confuse the preposition with the particle: ran up the hill (preposition — the hill is the object) vs. ran up a huge bill (particle — run up is the verb).

entries.meaning: The route preposition: it marks the waypoint between a start and a finish. Its second sense, a channel of transmission, is now the commoner one in everyday American writing — email, text, and courier all travel via something.
examples: The train runs to Sacramento via Stockton. (1)
They shipped it via Memphis to save two days. (1)
Confirm your appointment via the patient portal. (2)
I got the news via my sister-in-law. (2)
The virus spreads via contaminated water. (2)
Payment can be made via check or wire transfer. (2)

entries.pronunciation note: VEE-uh. Both are current in American English.
entries.русский: через, посредством — маршрутом через пункт; через канал, среду или посредника
entries.register: neutral to formal; standard in travel, logistics, and technical writing
entries.type: simple (from Latin via, "by way of the road")
entries.complement: noun phrase only. Gerunds (via emailing him) are awkward and better rewritten (by emailing him). Never a clause.
entries.pattern: [motion or transmission] via [place / route] · [action] via [medium or intermediary]
entries.contrast: Via names an intermediate point or a channel, never an origin or a destination — flew from Denver to Rome via Frankfurt has all three, and swapping via into either end position breaks the sentence. Against by for means: by is the ordinary word (by car, by mail), via is heavier and suggests a routed path. Against through: interchangeable for intermediaries (through a friend / via a friend), with via the more clinical choice. The full form by way of means the same and lives in the complex prepositions file.
entries.see also: through, by, across, by way of, past
